summary: Greylisting is the practice of temporarily rejecting mail from unknown senders as an anti-abuse measure. Legitimate servers retry later, while much spam software does not. This RFC describes the practice and its considerations in an applicability statement for SMTP.

plainLanguage.summary: A guard says come back in a few minutes to strangers. Real visitors return, but many troublemakers give up.

questions: what smtp code does greylisting use
what are the downsides of greylisting
subtitle: How and why mail servers temporarily turn away unknown senders, and what it costs legitimate mail.

tldr.problem: Spam software usually does not retry after a temporary SMTP failure, but there was no shared description or terminology for the anti-abuse practice that exploits this.
tldr.mechanism: Greylisting gives unknown or suspect senders a 4xx temporary failure and accepts them only if they retry within a window. The RFC defines the variants by SMTP phase and gives recommendations for tuple, timing, database and exceptions.
tldr.outcome: It is a cheap early filter, but it delays legitimate mail, penalizes clients that do not retry, and gets weaker against senders who retry.

facts.label: Recommended tuple
facts.value: IP, MAIL FROM, first RCPT TO

today: RFC 6647 is a Proposed Standard, published in June 2012, and the unit metadata shows no obsoleting or updating RFC. Its advice is based on IPv4 experience, as the text itself says.

sections.title: What Greylisting Is
sections.content:
Good email abuse handling separates good actors from bad ones. When a sender has no known reputation, greylisting gives it temporarily degraded service, typically for minutes or a few hours, until there is a basis for better service. In its narrow sense it means returning an SMTP temporary failure (4xx) for traffic from such sources.

The idea works because much spam comes from purpose-built software that supports only a constrained SMTP and does not retry after a temporary failure. The RFC calls greylisting cheap and early in the SMTP sequence, and says some spamware routes around it but much does not. It also aims to dispel confusion between greylisting and a temporary failure issued for any reason.
sections.plainLanguage: A doorman says 'not right now, try again soon' to people he does not know. Honest visitors come back. Many pranksters do not bother.

sections.title: Types of Greylisting
sections.content:
Greylisting keeps a database of attributes about the sending SMTP client, at its simplest its IP address. If the record is missing or not yet old enough (for example 30 minutes since the first attempt), the server returns a 4yz reply and waits for a retry. The RFC names variants by where in the session the decision happens.

  • Connection level: only the IP address is known. The server returns 421 and closes, or 4yz to all further commands.
  • HELO/EHLO: keyed on the source plus the HELO/EHLO parameter.
  • MAIL: source plus the return address.
  • RCPT: the recipient combined with the source, return address and other recipients.
  • DATA: on receipt of DATA or after the closing dot, which allows message headers, a digest or body analysis, at much higher cost.

Extra heuristics can target greylisting, such as applying it only to addresses on a DNS blacklist or to PTR names that look like dynamic addresses. Most systems also support exceptions for IP addresses, CIDR blocks, hosts or domains.
sections.plainLanguage: The doorman can check you at the gate, when you give your name, or after you hand over your parcel. Checking later learns more but takes more work.

sections.title: Benefits and Costs
sections.content:
The main benefit is that spamware generally does not retry, so it is less likely to succeed. The main cost is delay for legitimate mail. Some popular MTAs do not retry for an hour or more, and some do not retry at all. The RFC notes that non-retrying clients are not fully SMTP-capable, because a client is not entitled to know why it got a temporary failure.

The RFC argues email has always been best effort, so the cost is low compared with unwanted mail, yet delays can alter the flow of a mailing-list discussion. Renumbering makes known clients look new again. The database must be large and fast enough, and its record age matters: too short and good senders are repeatedly delayed, too long and a new spam campaign is no longer seen as unknown.

With exceptions for known senders, a steady state is reached where only mail from never-seen addresses is delayed. Greylisting on message content after DATA is substantially more expensive and is not typical practice.
sections.plainLanguage: Making strangers wait stops many troublemakers. But a friend you have not met yet also has to wait, and the guard needs a notebook to remember who came.

sections.title: Unintended Consequences
sections.content:
The RFC lists ways greylisting goes wrong for legitimate mail.

  • Two receiving servers that do not share a database each greylist the same client, amplifying the delay.
  • Multiple outbound MTAs, or a changing address from DHCP, make retries look like a new source.
  • DATA-level tuples change if the message is rewritten between attempts, and infrequent senders may be forgotten.
  • NAT can make later MTAs share the first one's pass.
  • Clients that never retry fail at once, and clients that treat 4yz as fatal can return mail or remove people from mailing lists.
  • An over-aggressive retry schedule can trigger rate limiting if records must reach a minimum age.

Alternate MX servers SHOULD share the same greylisting database, and a primary MX SHOULD let the other MX servers relay to it without greylisting. Address verification probes, from mailing list servers or from directory harvesting attacks, can be disrupted. Senders that mail just often enough to keep records alive are never caught after the first instance; pairing greylisting with a reputation service is suggested.
sections.plainLanguage: If a family uses two doors and the guards never talk to each other, you get sent away twice. Everyone needs to share the notebook.

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.content:
The RFC lists practices that are RECOMMENDED from experience.

  1. Use a tuple of IP address, MAIL FROM and the first RCPT TO; after a successful retry allow further traffic from that address.
  2. Define a retry window, by default SHOULD be one minute to 24 hours. Retries after its end count as new.
  3. Delete records for quiet addresses; the default SHOULD be at least one week.
  4. Border MTAs of one administrative domain SHOULD share a database and policy.
  5. Servers MAY track CIDR blocks such as /24 to cope with sender clusters.
  6. Provide a manual override list; known email providers that retry SHOULD bypass the filter.
  7. Do not apply greylisting to authenticated sessions or an ADMD's submission service for authenticated clients.

No specific 4yz code or reply text is recommended. The only two reasonable choices per SMTP are 421 to end the connection or 450 otherwise. To measure effectiveness, log what greylisting would have decided against spam versus legitimate verdicts, and check whether greylisted addresses are listed in popular DNS blacklists.
sections.plainLanguage: Good rules: remember visitors, let them return within a sensible time, forget them after a long while, and let known friends skip the queue.

sections.title: IPv6 and Security
sections.content:
The advice rests on years of experience with IPv4, so it clearly pertains to IPv4 only. The larger IPv6 address may let bad actors behave differently, may require different parameter choices, and might negate the benefit. The database would also likely be much larger.

On security, greylisting can harm timely delivery of financial, transactional or security-related mail, so consequences need careful thought. Excepted sources gain elevated access that malefactors may try to exploit. An attacker who knows the scheme could rotate client parameters to inflate the database until it causes denial of service, so implementers should configure a failure policy for when the database is attacked or unavailable.
sections.plainLanguage: The guard's notebook can be filled with fake visitors until it is useless, so the guard needs a plan for that, and the old rules may not suit the new, bigger addresses.
